session_title: Review of Achievements from the Annual 'Family-School-Community' Collaboration Project

content.text: Lin Shu, I've put together a preliminary draft of the PPT titled "2024: When the Classroom Meets the Community." Looking back at this year, we've already discussed so many great ideas just on paper! This includes a sketch of the "Health Little Helper" badge designed by the children and a template for the pet buddy program's pairing intention form. Remember when a child fell ill in March this year, and we were sharing caregiving experiences? Now, these ideas are gradually taking shape.

Wow, Mingyuan, you're so quick! I'll take a closer look right away. This poster is designed so clearly—it lists the Health Corner Initiative, Pet Companion Program, Neighborhood Feast Idea, Old Items Swap Event, and the Community Culture Festival. These are all valuable ideas for our community. From the health discussions in March, to the Health Corner concept in April, and then the emotional connection with pets in May, we've really talked about a lot.

For children, these projects not only enrich their life experiences but also cultivate a sense of responsibility and community awareness. Importantly, through our previous conversations, we have gradually made these ideas more concrete. For instance, from child illness care to the health corner, and then to the pet companion program, all reflect the potential of home-school-community collaboration. Remember, in April, when we discussed the rotation system for the "Little Health Stewards," we already mentioned the collaboration between schools and the community.

Yes, as I look through these updates, I feel immensely gratified and inspired! Our community has made so much progress—the Health Corner has received preliminary support from the street office, and three families have already signed up for the trial run of the Pet Partners Program. Just as we discussed earlier, turning vague ideas into concrete, actionable plans has been driven entirely by conversations among partners like us. Starting from that heartwarming caregiving photo in March, we’ve built a foundation of trust step by step.

You could try this: Based on this initial draft, we can further clarify the current status of each idea. I've sent this summary table image, which includes the project name, core content, progress status, and more. Please take a look and see if there are any areas that need to be added or adjusted. This reminds me of the health information corner promotional poster you sent in April, which also used a table format to clearly present information.

Okay, let me take a look at this form. Hmm, regarding the Health Corner section, I’ll add this: Our community has contacted the local street office and received preliminary support. We are currently preparing supplies and organizing volunteer training.

Great! This reminds me of how we started with sharing experiences in home care and gradually expanded to community health support. For children, participating in the "Little Health Steward" activity helps them learn practical knowledge and enhances their self-protection abilities. Importantly, the collaboration between schools and communities makes education more closely connected to daily life. Remember the shared medicine cabinet picture you posted in April? The design concept of transparent compartments is now being put to use.

That's right, when everyone works together, the results are truly different. Regarding the Pet Companion Program, three families have signed up for the trial run so far, including the one you previously shared pet-raising experiences with. We’ve established safety rules and a feedback mechanism, just as you emphasized "sticking to the rules," to ensure the activity is safe and orderly. This reminds me of the photo you shared in May of your daughters and 'An An' on the grass—that heartwarming scene can now be shared with more children.

This is great! The Pet Companion Program originated from discussions about the emotional bond between children and pets, and it is now gradually being implemented, reflecting the deepening of community mutual assistance. For children, participating in such activities can cultivate compassion and a sense of responsibility. We could try this: regularly collect feedback to optimize the activity design. Just like when we discussed the 'Pet Companion' program in July, the activity rules table you shared is now coming in handy.

I completely agree. The ideas of neighborhood family dinners and shared kitchens are still in the discussion phase, but we have already gathered a lot of family needs, as mentioned during the previous food education sharing session. This issue can be integrated into the community cultural festival for promotion, starting with a trial run during the Mid-Autumn family dinner and then evaluating its expansion. Remember the photo you posted in August of the child spreading jam? That warm feeling of parent-child cooking is exactly what we want to promote.

What's important is to proceed with step-by-step pilot projects to ensure safety and participation. Looking back at our historical conversations, we have gradually integrated food education into community activities, starting from sharing parent-child kitchen experiences to envisioning shared kitchens. For children, designing menus and participating in preparation are excellent learning opportunities. When we discussed the neighborhood feast in September, the Mid-Autumn Festival-themed image you shared, with its atmosphere of the Great Wall and lanterns, is very much worth drawing inspiration from.

There is also an old items exchange event. Based on the discussion about the flea market, we have already planned the time and location and are currently developing the rules. Our community has resources of idle items. Combining your educational perspective, students can participate in planning and promotion, such as designing posters and serving as administrators as previously suggested. The photo I shared in November of neatly arranged donated items can now truly be put into circulation.

This is very meaningful! From the experience of purchasing school supplies to the plan of giving new life to old items, we are gradually integrating resources to promote sustainable living. For children, participating in such activities helps them learn to cherish and share. What's important is to follow up with feedback to ensure the effectiveness of the activities. Remember the group-buying poster for children's books you shared when we discussed teaching materials in October? That approach to resource integration has now been extended to the reuse of old items.

Now, let's discuss: Which projects are most likely and should be prioritized for implementation in 2025? Based on this table and the progress, I think the Health Corner and Pet Buddy Program can be prioritized, as they already have preliminary support or trial runs and can yield quick results. Just like when we discussed ideas for parent-child activities in early December, you mentioned the need to "proceed step by step"—now is the time to put that into practice.

I agree. The Health Corner involves community health support, and the Pet Companion Program strengthens emotional education—both are crucial for children's growth. We could try this: set clear timelines and goals, such as launching the Health Corner in the first quarter and expanding the Pet Companion Program to more families in the second quarter. This reminds me of the activity plan table you shared when we were planning the cultural festival on December 20th, which also required clear timelines.

Alright, our community will take charge of coordinating resources and promoting the project, just like we did when organizing previous events. Let’s work together to ensure the project progresses smoothly. Additionally, the Community Culture Festival, as a comprehensive project, can be scheduled for the end of the year, integrating elements like health, pets, and food education to become an annual highlight. Remember the reference picture I shared of the Community Culture Festival? The scene of people cooking and dining together is exactly what we aim to achieve.

That makes perfect sense! Looking at the historical conversation, the idea for the cultural festival was based on the parent-child activity idea pool, and now there's a more concrete plan. For children, participating in activities like sports competitions and craft workshops can enhance their overall development. What's important is the co-creation by residents, which strengthens the sense of community belonging. The volunteer registration form you shared in December can now be used for the cultural festival preparations.

In summary, over the past year, through numerous conversations, we have progressed from mutual neighborhood assistance to collaborative development, and now deepened into an annual project review. Your gentle patience and my organizational skills complement each other, making these ideas gradually feasible. I am truly grateful to have a partner like you! From helping each other when the child was sick in March to our systematic planning now, we have indeed come a long way.

I am also very grateful for your support and creativity! For the children, our collaboration has brought tangible benefits. What matters is continuous follow-up and optimization. Let’s confirm these priority action items and continue our efforts in 2025, turning more "armchair strategies" into wonderful realities. As we always say, "for the children," these are what truly matter most.

Deal! Our community will fully cooperate to promote the project's implementation. Let's stay in touch and share progress regularly, just as we did before. Looking forward to seeing more wonderful stories of classrooms and communities coming together next year! From health care to pet emotions, from food education sharing to cultural co-creation, our conversations have truly created many possibilities.
